flawed_step: Line 0011 (with the whole second conjunct, f(n) != O(g(n)), never proved at all: lines 0017-0020 explicitly ask how to do it).
counterexample:
Counterexample to the inference in line 0011 (from 'f(n) > M*g(n)' and '0 <= M <= c1' conclude '0 <= c1*g(n) <= f(n)'):

Take g(n) = 1 for all n >= 1 and f(n) = n. Then f(n)/g(n) = n -> infinity, so the hypothesis of the statement holds and line 0009 applies.

Instantiate line 0009 with M = 1: n0 = 2 works, since for all n >= 2, f(n)/g(n) = n > 1 = M. Line 0010 then gives, for all n >= 2, f(n) = n > 1 = M*g(n). All true so far.

Now do exactly what line 0011 says: choose c1 with 0 <= M <= c1, e.g. c1 = 100 (this satisfies 0 <= 1 <= 100). The relation line 0011 claims to have 'defined' is 0 <= c1*g(n) <= f(n), i.e. 100 <= n for all n >= n0 = 2. At n = 5: c1*g(5) = 100*1 = 100, f(5) = 5, and 100 > 5. So c1*g(5) <= f(5) is FALSE, while every premise the step invokes (f(5) > M*g(5): 5 > 1, true; 0 <= M <= c1: 0 <= 1 <= 100, true) holds. Indeed the claimed relation fails at every n in {2,...,99}.

So the implication asserted in line 0011 is false as written: multiplying up gives f(n) > M*g(n), and a LARGER constant c1 >= M only weakens, never strengthens, the lower bound. The direction is inverted; the step needs 0 < c1 <= M (e.g. c1 = M) together with the n0 that the limit definition supplied for that M.

(Note the underlying theorem is true when g is eventually positive - taking c1 = M = 1 and n0 = 2 does prove f = Omega(g) in the example above - but the proof text's step 0011 does not establish it, and the second half of the claim, f(n) != O(g(n)), is not proved anywhere in the text: line 0017 asks how to prove it and line 0020 offers only an unverified 'main idea'.)
reasoning_summary: Line 0003 states the claim; lines 0006-0008 are headings. Line 0009 correctly restates lim f/g = infinity as: for all M > 0 there is n0 such that for all n >= n0, f(n)/g(n) > M. Line 0010 multiplies by g(n) to get f(n) > M*g(n); this is fine only if g(n) > 0, an assumption never stated but standard in this asymptotic setting, so I did not stop there. Line 0011 is the first step that definitively fails: it chooses c1 with 0 <= M <= c1 and claims this yields 0 <= c1*g(n) <= f(n). This inverts the inequality - a constant at least as large as M cannot be transferred into the lower bound f(n) > M*g(n). The explicit witness g == 1, f(n) = n, M = 1, n0 = 2, c1 = 100, n = 5 satisfies every premise while violating the asserted conclusion (100 > 5). The correct choice is c1 <= M. Consequently the Omega conclusion in line 0012 is not established by the argument given (even though it is true for eventually-positive g via c1 = M). Independently and decisively, the second conjunct of the statement to be proved, f(n) != O(g(n)), is never proved: lines 0017, 0019, and 0020 explicitly say the author does not know how and only sketches an unverified reductio. The submitted text is therefore not a valid proof of the stated claim.
